slides.title: From average to weighted
slides.kicker: The average gets a powerful upgrade this chapter
bullets: In earlier grades, the average told you the centre of a set of data — one number summarising the middle.
This chapter extends the average to a more general setting called the weighted average.
When data comes in groups of different sizes, a plain average of the group averages can mislead — weights fix that.

slides.title: The badminton academy puzzle
slides.kicker: Eleven trainees, two groups, one honest average
bullets: A badminton academy has 11 trainees: 8 seniors with average height 165.5 cm and 3 juniors with average height 149.33 cm.
Goal: find the average height of the whole group of 11 trainees.

slides.title: Method 1: the trap
slides.kicker: Adding two averages and halving — sounds fair, fails
bullets: It treats the seniors' average and the juniors' average as equally important.
But there are 8 seniors and only 3 juniors — Method 1 forgets the sizes, so 157.415 is wrong.
The correct average is the sum of all eleven heights divided by 11, which is 161.09 cm (Method 2).

slides.title: Shreyas weights the averages
slides.kicker: Multiply each average by its group size
bullets: Shreyas calculated ((165.5 × 8) + (149.33 × 3)) / (8 + 3) and got the correct answer.
165.5 × 8 = 1324 gives the sum of all senior heights; 149.33 × 3 = 448 gives the sum of all junior heights.
So (1324 + 448) / 11 = 1772 / 11 = 161.09 cm — exactly Method 2's answer.

items: Multiply each average by its count

slides.title: The general rule
slides.kicker: Two collections combine into one formula
bullets: Collection 1 has n values with average a; its sum is a × n. Collection 2 has m values with average b; its sum is b × m.
Combined average = (sum of both collections) / (total number of values) = (a n + b m) / (n + m).
The group sizes n and m act as weights — that is why this is called a weighted average.

items: Sums: a n and b m

slides.title: Bigger group pulls harder
slides.kicker: Watch the combined average lean to the seniors
bullets: The combined average 161.09 sits closer to the seniors' 165.5 than to the juniors' 149.33.
Reason: 8 of the 11 trainees are seniors, so their average carries the bigger weight.
If the groups were equal in size, plain averaging would work — weights matter only when sizes differ.

slides.title: Three families, six categories
bullets: Table 10.2 shows the average weekly expenditure, in rupees, of Families A, B and C.
Six categories: housing, food, education, transportation, healthcare and recreation.
Family B spends 0 on recreation while Family A spends 1940 on housing — the table is full of such stories.

slides.title: Two ways to cluster
bullets: A cluster-column chart stands columns side by side; the clusters can be chosen as categories or as families.
Choice 1 clusters by category: for each category, the three families' columns stand together.
Choice 2 clusters by family: for each family, its six category columns stand together.

slides.title: Choice 1: compare families
slides.kicker: Least housing? Most healthcare? Easy now
bullets: With categories clustered, comparing families inside one category takes a single glance.
Least spent on housing: Family C, only 950 rupees against A's 1940 and B's 1750.
Most spent on healthcare: Family A, 1770 rupees, ahead of C's 1300 and B's 1210.

slides.title: Choice 2: compare categories
slides.kicker: Inside one family, who leads the budget?
bullets: With families clustered, you can read one family's spending pattern across all six categories.
Family B's biggest expense is housing at 1750 rupees, then food at 1546 and education at 1500.
For Family A, healthcare at 1770 edges out food at 1700 — a question Choice 2 answers fastest.

slides.title: Totals hide in clusters
bullets: Questions like which family spent least overall are not direct in a cluster-column chart — you must add.
Totals: Family A = 8425 rupees, Family B = 7286 rupees, Family C = 7040 rupees.
So Family C spent least overall, even though Family B shows a zero in recreation — a close call!
Family C spent about 13.5 percent on housing: 950 of its 7040 total.

slides.title: Stacking columns solves it
slides.kicker: One column per family, total on top
bullets: A stacked column places one family's category segments on top of one another in a single column.
The full height of the stack shows the family's total weekly expenditure at a glance.
Each segment's size shows that category's share, making totals and percentage questions simple.

flashcards.back: An average where each group's average is multiplied by its size, so larger groups count more: (a n + b m) / (n + m).

flashcards.front: Why does averaging two group averages usually fail?
flashcards.back: It treats both averages as equally important even when group sizes differ, giving the smaller group too much say.

flashcards.front: In the badminton academy, what are the two group averages?
flashcards.back: 8 seniors average 165.5 cm and 3 juniors average 149.33 cm; the true group average is 1772 / 11 = 161.09 cm.

flashcards.front: What does multiplying an average by its count give you?
flashcards.back: The sum of all values in that group — for example 165.5 × 8 = 1324 cm, the seniors' total height.

flashcards.front: State the combined average formula for two collections.
flashcards.back: If the group averages are a and b with sizes n and m, the combined average is (a n + b m) / (n + m).

flashcards.front: Which group pulls a combined average towards itself?
flashcards.back: The larger group. The badminton average 161.09 lies closer to the seniors' 165.5 because 8 of the 11 trainees are seniors.

flashcards.front: What does Table 10.2 in this chapter show?
flashcards.back: The average weekly expenditure in rupees of Families A, B and C across six categories like housing, food and healthcare.

quiz.q: In the badminton academy, how are the 11 trainees split?
quiz.why: Example 1 lists 8 seniors with average 165.5 cm and 3 juniors with average 149.33 cm.

quiz.q: Method 1 computes (165.5 + 149.33) / 2. What value does it give?
quiz.why: 314.83 / 2 = 157.415, which is not the group's average because it ignores the group sizes.

quiz.q: Why does Method 1 fail for the badminton group?
options: It forgets the 8 versus 3 sizes and weighs both averages equally
It adds the heights in the wrong order
It uses centimetres instead of metres
It rounds the averages too early
quiz.why: The book says Method 1 treats the two averages equally, but there are many more seniors than juniors.

quiz.q: In Shreyas' calculation, what does 165.5 × 8 = 1324 represent?
options: The sum of all eight seniors' heights
The seniors' average in different units
The sum of all eleven heights
quiz.why: Average × count gives the group total, so 1324 cm is the sum of the seniors' eight heights.

quiz.q: When two groups of different sizes are combined, the combined average lies
options: closer to the larger group's average
exactly halfway between the two averages
closer to the smaller group's average
always equal to the larger group's average
quiz.why: Weights are the group sizes: 8 seniors pull the badminton average 161.09 towards 165.5.

quiz.q: A class has 20 students averaging 60 marks and 5 students averaging 80 marks. Find the combined average.
quiz.why: (60 × 20 + 80 × 5) / 25 = (1200 + 400) / 25 = 64; the sizes 20 and 5 decide the result.

quiz.q: How many spending categories does Table 10.2 track for each family?
quiz.why: Housing, food, education, transportation, healthcare and recreation — six categories.

quiz.q: Which family spent the least on housing?
quiz.why: Family C spent 950 rupees on housing, far below B's 1750 and A's 1940.

quiz.q: Which category did Family B spend the most on?
quiz.why: Family B's housing is 1750, above food 1546 and education 1500 — the tallest of its six columns.

quiz.q: Did Family A spend more on food or on healthcare?
quiz.why: Family A's healthcare is 1770 rupees and food is 1700, so healthcare edges it.

quiz.q: To answer 'which family spent the most on healthcare' fastest, which chart should you pick?
quiz.why: The book found Choice 1 best for questions like comparing families within one category.

quiz.q: Which family spent the least amount overall, according to the totals?
options: Family A, with the largest housing bill
All three spent the same overall
quiz.why: The totals are A 8425, B 7286 and C 7040; B's zero recreation does not make it the lowest.

quiz.q: About what percentage of Family C's weekly expenses went to housing?
quiz.why: Housing 950 of Family C's total 7040 gives 950 / 7040, about 13.5 percent.

examples.title: Badminton group average done right
examples.problem: In a badminton academy, 8 senior trainees have average height 165.5 cm and 3 junior trainees have average height 149.33 cm. Find the average height of the whole group of 11.
steps: Tempting shortcut: (165.5 + 149.33) / 2 = 314.83 / 2 = 157.415 cm. This is wrong — it weights both groups equally although they have 8 and 3 members.
Convert each average into a sum: average × count. Seniors: 165.5 × 8 = 1324 cm. Juniors: 149.33 × 3 = 448 cm.
Add the sums: 1324 + 448 = 1772 cm, the total height of all eleven trainees.
Divide by the total count: 1772 / 11 = 161.09 cm, matching Method 2's sum of all eleven heights divided by 11.
examples.answer: The group's average height is 1772 / 11, about 161.09 cm.

examples.title: Two collections, one formula
examples.problem: Collection 1 has n = 4 values with average a = 10 and Collection 2 has m = 6 values with average b = 20. Use the combined-average formula to find the average of all 10 values.
steps: Combined average = (a n + b m) / (n + m) = (40 + 120) / (4 + 6) = 160 / 10.
Notice the result leans towards 20 because the second collection has more values, 6 against 4.

examples.title: Weekly totals for the three families
examples.problem: Using Table 10.2, add up each family's average weekly expenditure across housing, food, education, transportation, healthcare and recreation, and find which family spent the least overall.
steps: Compare the totals: 7040 is less than 7286, which is less than 8425, so Family C spent the least even though Family B shows a zero in recreation.
examples.answer: Family A spends 8425, Family B 7286 and Family C 7040 rupees weekly; Family C is the lowest-spending family overall.

examples.title: Family C's housing share
examples.problem: Family C spends 950 rupees on housing out of a weekly total of 7040 rupees. What percentage of its expenditure goes to housing?
steps: Write the share as a fraction: housing / total = 950 / 7040.
Convert to a percentage: 0.135 × 100 is about 13.5 percent.
In a stacked column of Family C, housing appears as a thin bottom segment of roughly one-seventh of the height.
examples.answer: About 13.5 percent of Family C's weekly expenses go to housing.
